context: He has just explained, in Canto 17, that all the sins purged on the mountain are forms of misdirected love. It is night on the fourth terrace, and the poets cannot climb until morning.

quote: the blind who would be guides
note: Christ's phrase for false teachers: "the blind leading the blind" (Matthew 15:14). Virgil means those who teach that every love is good.

quote: created with the capacity to love
note: Virgil's account of how love happens follows the psychology of Aristotle as taught in medieval universities. The senses take in a thing, the mind forms an image of it, and if the soul leans toward that image, the leaning is love.

In medieval physics every element sought its natural place. Fire rose because its home was a sphere of fire high above the air, just below the moon. Desire carries the soul toward what it loves in the same way.

quote: all love is in itself praiseworthy
note: It is not certain whom Dante has in mind. Some commentators say the Epicureans, others the love poets of his own day, his younger self among them.

quote: however good the wax may be
note: A seal pressed into wax. The power to love is the wax, and it is always good. The particular love is the stamp pressed into it, which may be bad.

quote: the soul walks with no other foot
note: Dante's objection. If love is set off by things outside us, and love is the only thing that moves the soul, how can we be praised or blamed for where it goes? It is the question of Canto 16 again, asked now of love instead of the stars.

context: Virgil marks the limit of his own teaching. Reason can explain free will as far as philosophy goes. What depends on revelation is left for Beatrice, who speaks of it in Paradiso 5.

note: A term of medieval philosophy. A thing's substantial form is what makes it the kind of thing it is. The form of a human being is the soul, which is distinct from the body's matter but joined to it.

The truths the mind grasps without being taught, such as that a thing can't both be and not be. With them come the first desires, above all the desire for happiness. Both are simply given, like instinct, so they earn neither praise nor blame.
Reason, which judges each desire as it arises.
The answer to Dante's doubt. We do not choose what attracts us, but reason stands at the door like a guard and decides which loves to let in. Merit and guilt begin there, at consent.

quote: Those who reasoned to the foundation
note: The ancient philosophers, above all Aristotle and Plato. They saw that people are free to choose, and so they wrote about how to live.

Dante's word is "morality": moral philosophy as a whole, though Aristotle's Ethics, which Dante knew well, is its great example. There would be no point in teaching ethics to creatures who could not choose.
The moon was full when the journey began, several nights ago. Each night since it has risen later and thinner.
The waning moon, no longer round, looks like a rounded copper pail glowing with fire.
The whole sky turns from east to west each day. Against the background of the stars, the moon slowly slips the other way, from west to east.
Seen from Rome, the sun sets in that direction, to the west-southwest, in late autumn. The moon is now in the part of the zodiac where the sun is at that season.
Now Pietole, a village just outside Mantua, identified with Andes, where Virgil was born. Because of him it is more famous than Mantua itself.
Dante nods off on the terrace of sloth. The sin of the place touches him just before its souls burst in.
Two rivers near Thebes, in Greece. The Thebans worshipped Bacchus by running in wild crowds along their banks at night, carrying torches.
The god of wine, called Dionysus by the Greeks. Thebes was his mother's city and the center of his cult.
The penance of the slothful. Those who were slow to do good now run without rest, day and night. This is the only terrace where the souls recite no prayer: their haste is their prayer.

context: The first example of zeal. After the angel told her she would bear Christ, Mary "went with haste into the hill country" to visit her cousin Elizabeth (Luke 1:39). On every terrace the first example of the virtue comes from her life.

The second example of zeal. In 49 BC, at the start of the civil war, Caesar would not wait for the siege of Marseilles to end. He left part of his army there and raced on to Spain, where he defeated Pompey's forces.

note: Now Lleida, in Catalonia, where Pompey's generals surrendered to Caesar. Dante knew the campaign from Lucan's poem on the civil war.
Eagerness to do good makes God's grace grow green again, like a plant watered.

quote: if you take our justice for rudeness
note: The soul answers without stopping. Their just penance is never to stand still, so even courtesy has to be shouted on the run.
San Zeno is the great abbey church of Verona, the city where Dante found his first refuge in exile. Nothing certain is known of this abbot. He is often identified as a Gherardo who died in 1187.

context: In 1162 he razed Milan to the ground for rebelling against him. Whether "good" is sincere or ironic is disputed. Dante believed in the empire's authority over the Italian cities.

quote: one man already has one foot in the grave
note: Alberto della Scala, lord of Verona, who died in 1301, the year after the journey. He was the father of Bartolomeo and Cangrande della Scala, Dante's hosts and patrons in exile.

Giuseppe della Scala, Alberto's illegitimate son, who was lame. In 1292 his father forced him on the monks as abbot of San Zeno. Church law barred the illegitimate and the physically impaired from such an office.
Biting at it: denouncing it with examples of sloth punished. Each terrace pairs examples of the virtue, which spur the souls on, with examples of the sin, which rein them in.

The Israelites, who crossed the Red Sea out of Egypt. In the desert they lost heart and complained, and God decreed that the whole generation would die there. Their children entered the Promised Land (Numbers 14).
The river that bounds the Promised Land on the east. Of the adults who left Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb lived to cross it.

context: In Book 5 of the Aeneid, the Trojans who were tired of wandering stayed behind in Sicily. They had no part in the founding of Rome.

note: Dante falls asleep at the end of his second day on the mountain. The dream is told at the start of Canto 19.
